questions.q: Which business applications hold the data you would least like to see leaked?
questions.why: Ranks tenants by what is at stake, not by size.
questions.need: The applications holding the most sensitive data are known
questions.how: Rank tenants by the data they hold
questions.listen: Two or three named applications; "all of them" means nobody has ranked them.
questions.probe: Who owns each of those applications on the business side?

questions.q: How many SaaS tenants do you have, including ones teams bought on a card?
questions.why: Shadow tenants are the ones with no one watching.
questions.need: Every SaaS tenant is known, card purchases included
questions.how: Find tenants from sign-ins and expenses, and connect them
questions.listen: The card statements are the honest list; the IT list is usually shorter.
questions.probe: Who could pull the list of SaaS paid for by card last year?

questions.q: Do you know which third-party apps can read your mail or files today?
questions.why: OAuth grants are a common, quiet path to data.
questions.need: Third-party apps with access to mail or files are known and approved
questions.how: Review app grants and remove the risky ones
questions.listen: Third-party apps with read access to mail or files are a quiet way out for data.
questions.probe: Who approves an app's access, and has any been removed?

questions.q: Is strong sign-in enforced for everyone, admins included, with no exceptions list?
questions.why: Exceptions lists tend to grow and are where accounts get taken.
questions.need: Strong sign-in protects everyone, admins included
questions.how: Close the exceptions one group at a time
questions.listen: "Except" again: admins without strong sign-in are the accounts attackers want.
questions.probe: Which admins are on the exceptions list, and why?

questions.q: How do you find files shared with anyone who has the link?
questions.why: Public links are the most frequent SaaS data leak.
questions.need: Files shared with anyone who has the link are found and reviewed
questions.how: Find public links and agree a policy
questions.listen: Public links on sensitive data are the leak most often found by someone else.
questions.probe: When did someone last find a public link that should not have been?

questions.q: Who reviews admin roles, and how often?
questions.why: Standing admin rights outlive the people and projects that needed them.
questions.need: Admin roles are reviewed on a schedule
questions.how: Set a review cycle with a named reviewer
questions.listen: Reviewed on a schedule, with admins removed; too many global admins is the common finding.
questions.probe: How many people hold the highest admin role today?

questions.q: When a risky setting is found, which team owns the fix?
questions.why: SaaS settings often belong to the business, not to IT.
questions.need: Every risky setting has a team that owns the fix
questions.listen: A team named per application; security finding it and nobody fixing it is the usual stall.
questions.probe: What happened to the last risky setting that was found?

questions.q: What would a clean audit of these tenants mean for you this year?
questions.why: Ties posture work to a date the sponsor already cares about.
questions.need: A clean audit of these tenants is within reach this year
questions.how: Agree what the auditor will ask, and close the gaps
questions.listen: An audit with a date makes this a project with a deadline.
questions.probe: What did the last audit find, and is it closed?
